sentences.text: Hamipterus is a monotypic genus, meaning it contains only one known species, Hamipterus tianshanensis.
Adult specimens of this pterosaur exhibited a wingspan that varied between 1.5 and 3.5 meters.
A distinctive hook-shaped process is present on the dentary bone, which forms the front part of the lower jaw.
The rear upper portion of the skull features a prominent crest located on the central supraoccipital bone.
Teeth in this animal were covered by very thin enamel that extended over only about half of the tooth crown.
The upper arm bone, or humerus, contains a hole near the base of the muscle attachment ridge.
A spine-like projection points downward on the lower external carpal bone found in the wrist area.
Both the very tip of the snout and the jaw itself are slightly expanded outward.
Excavations uncovered eleven blocks of fossils representing at least forty individuals, some preserving soft tissue like horn sheaths.
Five uncrushed eggs were discovered at the same site alongside the adult skeletons.
The species was formally named and described in 2014 by a research team led by Wang Xiaolin and Alexander Kellner.
The specific name tianshanensis honors the Tian Shan mountain range where the fossils were originally found.
The holotype, which is the single specimen the species description is based on, is a skull likely belonging to a female.
To date, four separate fossil occurrences of this genus have been recorded by scientists.
A later study by Wang and colleagues in 2026 described an articulated forelimb from Lower Cretaceous rocks in Xinjiang, China.
The abundance of fossils allowed researchers to construct a growth series illustrating how the animals developed through their life stages.
This large collection of individuals enabled the establishment of an ontogenetic series showing development as the creatures matured.
Scientists hypothesized that sexual dimorphism existed, with larger males sporting bigger crests than smaller females.
It is presumed that clear sexual dimorphism occurred, where larger specimens with large crests were males and smaller ones with smaller crests were females.
Hamipterus is classified within the suborder Pterodactyloidea and the group Pteranodontoidea.
Cladistic analyses have recovered this genus within the family Hamipteridae.
The taxon is placed within Pterodactyloidea and the clade Pteranodontoidea.
Hamipterus was an extinct pterosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in northwestern China.
The species inhabited the Valanginian stage, a time period spanning from 137.05 to 132.6 million years ago.
A 2021 study disputes earlier claims of parental care, showing that young Hamipterus did not differ significantly from other flight-capable hatchlings.
A cladistic analysis could not precisely resolve its evolutionary relationships with Istiodactylus, Ludodactylus, and the family Anhangueridae.
If the presumption of sexual dimorphism is correct, it would refute the hypothesis that only males possessed crests in pterosaurs.
